Verify

/VAIR-uh-fye/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Verify means to make sure or demonstrate that something is true, accurate, or justified by checking it.

Election clerks verify each mailed ballot's signature against the voter's registration card before the vote is counted.

Worked Example

Before running the story, the reporter spent two days working to verify every date and dollar figure against bank records and public files.

The reporter doesn't just trust her notes — she checks each fact against reliable outside sources (bank records, public files) to make sure it's accurate. That checking-against-a-trusted-standard is what verify means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

confirm: Confirm means to establish that something is true, often with a single acknowledgment — a source confirms the story, a click confirms the booking. Verify emphasizes the checking itself: comparing a fact against a trusted standard until you are sure. You confirm by saying yes; you verify by checking it through.

authenticate: Authenticate means to prove that something is genuine rather than fake — a signature, a painting, a login. Verify is broader: to check any fact or claim for accuracy against a reliable source. You authenticate the object itself; you verify what is said about it.

substantiate: Substantiate means to back a claim with supporting evidence — the burden falls on whoever made the claim. Verify is the checker's move: testing a statement against a trusted standard to see whether it holds. You substantiate your own account; someone else verifies it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

disprove: to show that something is false

debunk: to expose a claim as untrue

Where it sits · how thoroughly the truth is established — check → verify → prove

check vs. verify: To check something is just to glance it over; to verify is to check it carefully against a trusted source until you're sure it's accurate.

prove vs. verify: To prove goes further than to verify — proving establishes truth so firmly that it convinces even the people who doubted it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ver-

Root — ver-: true (Latin verus)

Suffix — -ify

Suffix — -ify: to make, to cause to be (from Latin facere, 'to make')

Put it together

Put it together: Verify is literally 'to make true' — the Latin root verus ('true') plus -ify ('make') builds a verb meaning to establish that something really is true.

Use the root in a new word: veritable

Use the root in a new word: veritable: Veritable means 'true to the name' — after the snowstorm, the backyard was a veritable mountain range of drifts.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral / Procedural

You verify facts, figures, identities, sources, and accounts — always against something reliable. It's a step more formal than 'check': checking can be a quick glance, but verifying implies comparing against a trusted standard. You can verify a thing ('verify the address') or verify that something is so ('verify that the name matches').
